summary.text: The Taylor sum is rewritten as the weighted binomial coefficient \([x^B]W(x)(1+x)^A\), with \(W(x)=(1-x^2)/(1+x+x^2)\), and the expansion \((1+x)^p=1+x^p+pH(x)\), where \(1+x+x^2\mid H\) and \(H\) is palindromic, reduces the claim to its nonconstant Frobenius-error terms.  After contracting to coefficients whose indices are multiples of \(p\), these terms are antisymmetric; pairing them gives a factor \(p^{3e}\) from the falling-factorial factors when \(p^e\mid A,B\), while \(j-v_p(j!)\ge3\) for \(j\ge3\) (and exact cancellation for \(j\le2\)) supplies the remaining \(p^3\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 c(x)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}.
\]
Thus \(c(x)=1+xc(x)^2\). We prove the stronger statement for the integer-parameter family obtained from \(c(x)^{mn}\), and then put \(m=4\).

Throughout, for an integer \(r\) and a nonnegative integer \(s\), write
\[
 \binom rs=\frac{r(r-1)\cdots(r-s+1)}{s!}\in\mathbb Z,
\]
with \(\binom r0=1\). Also write
\[
 z^{\underline s}=z(z-1)\cdots(z-s+1)
\]
for a falling factorial.

## 1. Rewriting the truncated Catalan sum

Define the polynomial version of the coefficient of \(c(x)^r\) by
\[
 C_r(0)=1,
\]
and, for \(s>0\),
\[
 C_r(s)=\binom{r+2s}{s}-2\binom{r+2s-1}{s-1}.
\tag{1}
\]
Pascal's identity gives the equivalent expression
\[
 C_r(s)=\binom{r+2s-1}{s}-\binom{r+2s-1}{s-1}.
\tag{2}
\]
The standard recurrence
\[
 (s+1)\binom r{s+1}=(r-s)\binom rs
\tag{3}
\]
for generalized binomial coefficients then shows that
\[
 (r+s)C_r(s)=r\binom{r+2s-1}{s}.
\tag{4}
\]
When \(r+s\ne0\), this is the familiar formula
\[
 C_r(s)=\frac r{r+s}\binom{r+2s-1}{s}.
\tag{5}
\]
It is also the coefficient of \(x^s\) in \(c(x)^r\). Indeed, putting \(u=c-1\), we have \(u=x(1+u)^2\), and Lagrange inversion gives, for \(s>0\),
\[
 [x^s](1+u)^r
 =\frac r s[t^{s-1}](1+t)^{r-1+2s}
 =\frac r s\binom{r+2s-1}{s-1},
\]
which is equal to (1)--(2). This polynomial formula remains meaningful at the removable singular value \(r=-s\); direct substitution in (2) gives
\[
 C_{-s}(s)=-1 \qquad(s>0).
\tag{6}
\]

The integer-division definition used for the generalized sequence takes the quotient in (5), with quotient by zero equal to zero. Consequently it differs from \(C_r(s)\) only in the singular case:
\[
 G_r(s)=C_r(s)+
 \begin{cases}
 1,&s>0\text{ and }r+s=0,\\
 0,&\text{otherwise}.
 \end{cases}
\tag{7}
\]
For the OEIS sequence, where \(r=4n>0\), this exceptional case never occurs, so \(G_r(s)=C_r(s)=[x^s]c(x)^r\).

We next convert the sum of the \(C_r(s)\)'s to one weighted binomial coefficient. Define
\[
 w_0=1,
 \qquad
 w_t=\begin{cases}
 2,&t>0\text{ and }3\mid t,\\
 -1,&t>0\text{ and }3\nmid t,
 \end{cases}
\]
and let
\[
 W(x)=\sum_{t\ge0}w_tx^t.
\]
The sequence starts \(1,-1,-1,2,-1,-1,2,\ldots\), and direct multiplication gives
\[
 W(x)(1+x+x^2)=1-x^2.
\tag{8}
\]
For \(A\in\mathbb Z\) and \(B\ge0\), define
\[
 \mathcal B(A,B)=[x^B]W(x)(1+x)^A,
\tag{9}
\]
where \((1+x)^A=\sum_{s\ge0}\binom Asx^s\) if \(A\) is negative.

We claim
\[
 \sum_{s=0}^n C_r(s)=\mathcal B(r+2n,n).
\tag{10}
\]
This can be proved by induction on \(n\). Both sides equal \(1\) at \(n=0\). For the induction step, use
\[
 (1+x)^{r+2n+2}=(1+x)^{r+2n}(1+x)^2
\]
and (8), equivalently
\[
 W(x)(1+x)^2=xW(x)+(1-x)(1+x).
\tag{11}
\]
After multiplying (11) by \((1+x)^{r+2n}\) and taking the coefficient of \(x^{n+1}\), one obtains
\[
 \mathcal B(r+2n+2,n+1)-\mathcal B(r+2n,n)
 =\binom{r+2n+1}{n+1}-\binom{r+2n+1}{n},

a quantity equal to \(C_r(n+1)\) by (2). This proves (10).

For positive \(n\), set
\[
 a_m(n)=\sum_{s=0}^nG_{mn}(s).
\]
In the exceptional term in (7), the conditions \(0<s\le n\) and \(mn+s=0\) can hold only when \(m=-1\) and \(s=n\): if \(m\ge0\) the sum cannot be zero, while if \(m\le-2\), then \(-mn\ge2n>n\). Hence (7) and (10) give
\[
 a_m(n)=\mathcal B((m+2)n,n)+\delta_{m,-1},
\tag{12}
\]
where \(\delta_{m,-1}\) is \(1\) for \(m=-1\) and \(0\) otherwise. If one uses the actual Taylor coefficient at the removable singularity instead of the integer-division convention, the same formula holds without the delta term. In either interpretation, the extra term is independent of \(n\), so it cancels in every congruence under consideration.

Thus it remains to prove a supercongruence for \(\mathcal B(A,B)\).

## 2. The Frobenius quotient and its symmetries

Fix a prime \(p\ge5\), and put
\[
 Q(x)=1+x+x^2.
\]
Define
\[
 F(x)=(1+x)^p-1-x^p.
\]
Every intermediate binomial coefficient \(\binom pi\), \(0<i<p\), is divisible by \(p\), so there is a polynomial \(H(x)\in\mathbb Z[x]\) such that
\[
 F(x)=pH(x).
\tag{13}
\]
It has the following properties:
\[
 \deg H\le p,\qquad H(0)=0,\qquad x^pH(1/x)=H(x),\qquad Q(x)\mid H(x).
\tag{14}
\]
The first and second properties are immediate from (13), and the reciprocal symmetry follows because
\[
 x^pF(1/x)=F(x).
\]
It remains to justify the divisibility by \(Q\).

Since \(p\ge5\) is prime, \(p\equiv1\) or \(5\pmod6\). Work modulo \(Q\), and denote the class of \(x\) again by \(x\). The relation \(1+x+x^2=0\) implies
\[
 x^3=1,\qquad (1+x)^3=-1,

together with \(x^6=(1+x)^6=1\). Reducing exponents modulo \(6\), one checks in both cases \(p\equiv1,5\pmod6\) that
\[
 (1+x)^p=1+x^p.
\]
Therefore \(Q\mid F\). Since \(F=pH\), \(Q\) is monic, and multiplication by the nonzero integer \(p\) cannot create divisibility by a monic polynomial, it follows that \(Q\mid H\). This proves (14).

For a polynomial \(R\) of degree at most \(N\), call it symmetric about \(N\) if
\[
 x^NR(1/x)=R(x),
\]
and antisymmetric about \(N\) if the left side equals \(-R(x)\). Thus (14) says that \(H\) is symmetric about \(p\). Also \(Q\) is symmetric about \(2\), while \(1-x^2\) is antisymmetric about \(2\).

For every \(j\ge1\), the formal series \(W(x)H(x)^j\) is in fact a polynomial. Indeed, write \(H=QR\). By (8),
\[
 P_j(x):=W(x)H(x)^j=(1-x^2)R(x)H(x)^{j-1}.
\tag{15}
\]
It satisfies
\[
 \deg P_j\le pj,\qquad P_j(0)=0,
 \qquad x^{pj}P_j(1/x)=-P_j(x).
\tag{16}
\]
For completeness, the antisymmetry can be seen without making any assumption about the exact degree of \(R\). Multiplying (15) by \(Q\) gives
\[
 QP_j=(1-x^2)H^j.
\]
The right side is antisymmetric about \(2+pj\), because \(1-x^2\) is antisymmetric about \(2\) and \(H^j\) is symmetric about \(pj\). The factor \(Q\) is symmetric about \(2\), so cancellation of the nonzero polynomial \(Q\) yields the last relation in (16). The degree bound follows from the same identity, and the constant term vanishes because \(H(0)=0\).

Now retain only the coefficients whose exponents are multiples of \(p\). Write
\[
 V_j(y)=\sum_{\ell\ge0}[x^{p\ell}]P_j(x)y^\ell.
\tag{17}
\]
By (16), \(\deg V_j\le j\). If \(v_\ell=[y^\ell]V_j\), then
\[
 v_0=v_j=0,
 \qquad v_{j-\ell}=-v_\ell\quad(0\le\ell\le j).
\tag{18}
\]
These antisymmetric coefficients are the source of the third power of the modulus.

## 3. The antisymmetric falling-factorial lemma

We first prove an elementary divisibility statement. Let \(q\) divide both integers \(B\) and \(C\), where in the application \(B,C\) are nonnegative. Suppose integers \(v_0,\ldots,v_j\) satisfy (18). Then
\[
 q^3\mid
 \sum_{\ell=0}^j
 v_\ell B^{\underline\ell}C^{\underline{j-\ell}}.
\tag{19}
\]

For \(s>0\), factor
\[
 z^{\underline s}=zT_s(z),
 \qquad T_s(z)=\prod_{i=1}^{s-1}(z-i).
\tag{20}
\]
Since \(q\mid B,C\), polynomial evaluation gives
\[
 T_s(B)\equiv T_s(0)\pmod q,
 \qquad T_s(C)\equiv T_s(0)\pmod q.
\tag{21}
\]
The terms \(\ell=0\) and \(\ell=j\) in (19) vanish by (18). For every remaining term, both falling factorials have the form (20). The product \(BC\) contributes \(q^2\), and replacing the two tail factors by their values at zero changes their product by a multiple of \(q\). Hence modulo \(q^3\), the sum in (19) is
\[
 BC\sum_{\ell=0}^jv_\ell T_\ell(0)T_{j-\ell}(0),
\tag{22}
\]
where the endpoint terms may harmlessly be included because their coefficients are zero. The summand indexed by \(j-\ell\) is the negative of the summand indexed by \(\ell\), by (18). Thus the sum in (22) is zero, proving (19).

There is also a small-\(j\) strengthening that will be needed below. If \(j\le2\), then every \(v_\ell\) is zero: the endpoints vanish, and the only possible interior coefficient, when \(j=2\), satisfies \(v_1=-v_1\), hence is zero over \(\mathbb Z\). Therefore the sum in (19) is exactly zero for \(j\le2\).

We combine this with a binomial identity. Let \(0\le B\le A\), \(j\le A\), and let \(V(y)=\sum_{\ell=0}^jv_\ell y^\ell\). Expanding the indicated coefficient and using factorial definitions gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 &j!\binom Aj [y^B]V(y)(1+y)^{A-j}\\
 &\qquad=\binom AB
 \sum_{\ell=0}^j
 v_\ell B^{\underline\ell}(A-B)^{\underline{j-\ell}}.
 \end{aligned}
\tag{23}
\]
Indeed, the coefficient on the left is a sum of
\(v_\ell\binom{A-j}{B-\ell}\), interpreted as zero when \(\ell>B\); term by term,
\[
 j!\binom Aj\binom{A-j}{B-\ell}
 =\binom AB B^{\underline\ell}(A-B)^{\underline{j-\ell}}.
\]
If one of the displayed binomial coefficients is outside its natural range, both sides are zero, so (23) remains valid without extra restrictions on \(\ell\).

Suppose now that \(p^e\mid A\) and \(p^e\mid B\). Since \(B\le A\), we also have \(p^e\mid A-B\). Apply (19) with \(q=p^e\), \(C=A-B\), and coefficients satisfying (18). The sum on the right of (23) is divisible by \(p^{3e}\). Therefore, for
\[
 T=p^j\binom Aj[y^B]V(y)(1+y)^{A-j},
\]
identity (23) shows
\[
 j!T\quad\text{is divisible by}\quad p^{j+3e}.
\tag{24}
\]

For \(j\ge3\), we use the elementary valuation estimate
\[
 v_p(j!)+3\le j.
\tag{25}
\]
To see it, the usual bound from Legendre's formula gives
\[
 (p-1)v_p(j!)<j.
\]
As \(p-1\ge4\), we have \(4v_p(j!)<j\). If the valuation is zero, (25) follows from \(j\ge3\); if it is positive, the same strict inequality implies (25). Subtracting \(v_p(j!)\) from (24) and using (25) gives
\[
 p^{3(e+1)}\mid T.
\tag{26}
\]
For \(j=1,2\), the small-\(j\) observation says that the sum in (23) is exactly zero, hence \(T=0\), and (26) again holds. We have proved:

**Weighted-term lemma.** If \(p\ge5\) is prime, \(B\le A\), \(p^e\mid A,B\), and \(V\) has degree at most \(j\) with coefficients satisfying (18), then
\[
 p^{3(e+1)}\mid
 p^j\binom Aj[y^B]V(y)(1+y)^{A-j}.
\tag{27}
\]

## 4. Supercongruence for nonnegative upper parameter

Assume for the moment that \(A,B\) are nonnegative, \(B\le A\), and \(p^e\mid A,B\). From (13),
\[
 (1+x)^p=1+x^p+pH(x).

\]
Raising to the \(A\)-th power yields
\[
 (1+x)^{pA}
 =\sum_{j=0}^A p^j\binom AjH(x)^j(1+x^p)^{A-j}.
\tag{28}
\]
Multiply by \(W(x)\) and extract the coefficient of \(x^{pB}\). This expresses \(\mathcal B(pA,pB)\) as the sum of the corresponding terms in (28).

The \(j=0\) term is exactly \(\mathcal B(A,B)\). To see this, note that \(p\ne3\), and therefore
\[
 w_{pt}=w_t\qquad(t\ge0),
\tag{29}
\]
because multiplication by \(p\) neither creates nor destroys divisibility by \(3\), and \(pt=0\) exactly when \(t=0\). Since \((1+x^p)^A\) contains only powers divisible by \(p\), (29) gives
\[
 [x^{pB}]W(x)(1+x^p)^A
 =[y^B]W(y)(1+y)^A
 =\mathcal B(A,B).
\tag{30}
\]

For \(j\ge1\), replace \(W(x)H(x)^j\) by the polynomial \(P_j(x)\) of (15), and let \(V_j\) be its contraction (17). Since the second factor contains only powers of \(x^p\),
\[
 [x^{pB}]P_j(x)(1+x^p)^{A-j}
 =[y^B]V_j(y)(1+y)^{A-j}.
\tag{31}
\]
The coefficients of \(V_j\) satisfy (18), so the weighted-term lemma shows that every \(j\ge1\) term in (28), after coefficient extraction, is divisible by \(p^{3(e+1)}\). Together with (30), this proves
\[
 \mathcal B(pA,pB)\equiv\mathcal B(A,B)
 \pmod{p^{3(e+1)}}
\tag{32}
\]
for nonnegative \(A,B\) with \(B\le A\) and \(p^e\mid A,B\).

## 5. Extension to an arbitrary integer upper parameter

The eventual upper parameter is \((m+2)B\), which can be negative, so we extend (32) to all \(A\in\mathbb Z\).

We use the following continuity fact. If \(a,b,M\in\mathbb Z\), \(D\ge0\), and
\[
 D!M\mid a-b,
\tag{33}
\]
then for every \(s\le D\),
\[
 M\mid\binom as-\binom bs.
\tag{34}
\]
Indeed, let \(f_s(z)=z(z-1)\cdots(z-s+1)\). The polynomial difference \(f_s(a)-f_s(b)\) is divisible by \(a-b\). Also \(s!\mid D!\), so (33) implies that \(s!M\) divides \(a-b\), and hence divides \(f_s(a)-f_s(b)=s!(\binom as-\binom bs)\). Cancelling the nonzero integer \(s!\) proves (34).

Because \(\mathcal B(a,B)\) is a linear combination, with fixed integer weights, of \(\binom as\) for \(0\le s\le B\), it follows that
\[
 B!M\mid a-b
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 \mathcal B(a,B)\equiv\mathcal B(b,B)\pmod M.
\tag{35}
\]

Now let \(A\in\mathbb Z\), let \(B\ge0\), assume \(p^e\mid A\) and \(p^e\mid B\), and put
\[
 M=p^{3(e+1)},
 \qquad L=(pB)!M.
\]
Choose a nonnegative integer \(A'\ge B\) satisfying
\[
 A'\equiv A\pmod L.
\tag{36}
\]
Such an \(A'\) exists: choose any nonnegative representative of the residue class of \(A\) modulo the positive integer \(L\), then add a sufficiently large multiple of \(L\).

Since \(p^e\mid M\), congruence (36) and \(p^e\mid A\) imply \(p^e\mid A'\). We may therefore apply (32) to \(A',B\):
\[
 \mathcal B(pA',pB)\equiv\mathcal B(A',B)\pmod M.
\tag{37}
\]
On the high side, \((pB)!M=L\) divides \(pA'-pA\), so (35), with lower index \(pB\), gives
\[
 \mathcal B(pA,pB)\equiv\mathcal B(pA',pB)\pmod M.
\tag{38}
\]
On the low side, \(B!\mid(pB)!\), and hence \(B!M\mid A'-A\); another application of (35) gives
\[
 \mathcal B(A',B)\equiv\mathcal B(A,B)\pmod M.
\tag{39}
\]
Combining (37)--(39), we obtain the key result in full generality:
\[
 \boxed{\mathcal B(pA,pB)\equiv\mathcal B(A,B)
 \pmod{p^{3(e+1)}}}
\tag{40}
\]
whenever \(A\in\mathbb Z\), \(B\ge0\), and \(p^e\) divides both \(A\) and \(B\).

## 6. Application to the Catalan sequence

Let \(m\in\mathbb Z\), let \(n,k>0\), and write \(k=e+1\). Set
\[
 B=np^e,
 \qquad A=(m+2)B.
\]
Both \(A\) and \(B\) are divisible by \(p^e\). Formula (40) therefore gives
\[
 \mathcal B\bigl((m+2)np^{e+1},np^{e+1}\bigr)
 \equiv
 \mathcal B\bigl((m+2)np^e,np^e\bigr)
 \pmod{p^{3(e+1)}}.
\tag{41}
\]
By (12), the two sides are respectively \(a_m(np^{e+1})\) and \(a_m(np^e)\), up to the same constant \(\delta_{m,-1}\). This constant cancels, so
\[
 a_m(np^k)\equiv a_m(np^{k-1})\pmod{p^{3k}}.
\tag{42}
\]

Finally take \(m=4\). Then there is no exceptional term, and
\[
 a_4(N)=\sum_{s=0}^N[x^s]c(x)^{4N}

a is exactly the value at \(x=1\) of the degree-\(N\) Taylor truncation of \(c(x)^{4N}\), namely OEIS A333096. Thus, for every prime \(p\ge5\) and all positive integers \(n,k\),
\[
 \boxed{a(np^k)\equiv a(np^{k-1})\pmod{p^{3k}}}.
\]
This proves the conjectured supercongruence.
